2.text: by making offerings to the household spirits. She declared that an unfamiliar

3.text: odor given off by the case made her feel giddy and sick; “since it has seen

4.text: so many strange countries and hearths,” was added by way of explanation.

5.text: On the other hand, my books and instruments, although they have been in

6.text: still stranger countries, were not objected to at all; nor were the provisions

7.text: of civilization — canned meats, fruit, vegetables, sugar, etc. — rejected on

9.text: Regarding taste there are also some peculiar features. Thus the Chukchee

10.text: generally do not care for salt; many of them have, in fact, a decided aversion

11.text: to it, declaring that it is bitter and tastes of sea-water. The Lamut, on the

12.text: contrary, relish salt, and, when it is at hand, often use it with their tea. Some

13.text: of the Chukchee have also an aversion toward soft bread, which to them

14.text: tastes too sour. They will consume only hard biscuit, especially unsalted hard-

15.text: tack. The Russianized natives, on the contrary, who are used to baked bread,

16.text: find ship-biscuit tasteless. The desire for fat seems to be innate in the Chuk-

17.text: chee. I saw an infant not a year old that cried every time an oil lamp was

18.text: carried past his head. As the oil was very rancid, he evidently recognized

19.text: it by its odor, and wanted some of it. To grown people an admixture of fat

20.text: will improve the taste of all spoiled provisions: therefore putrid meat which

21.text: has been stored in summer is usually consumed with oil or tallow. The

22.text: consumption of fat, however, has some limitations. Many persons, especially

23.text: women, cannot eat the blubber of the male rough-seal (Phoca hispida) because

24.text: of its disgusting odor. Among the Reindeer people the marrow of the wild

25.text: reindeer-buck is considered the best food in the world. Notwithstanding this,

26.text: most of the people are not able “to break the joints” (i. e., to eat the marrow)

27.text: of a whole animal, and some are contented with a single leg. There is a

28.text: special term for the taste of food that is excessively fat and sweet, — nɪñɪˊrñuqin

30.text: The Chukchee scale of colors is also somewhat peculiar. The best-known

31.text: colors are white (niˊlhᴀqin), black (nuˊuqin), red (nɪčêˊʟ̣oqên), gray (čêvaˊro).

32.text: Among reindeer-skins the color “yellowish” (ɪplɪˊlɪ) is also recognized. Occasion-

33.text: ally this term may be applied to other skins, but never to anything else.

34.text: Other colors are not strictly defined, but are included among the preceding,

35.text: or described by comparison with various existing objects. Thus we have the

37.text: “Weed-like” (nŭwtɪčɪˊrrᴀqên), an indefinite term, that is applied to all

38.text: the tints of green, yellow, or even blue when not very deep. The usual

39.text: summer color of the weeds on the tundra is green for the leaves and the

40.text: tip-ends of the stalks, but the lower parts of the plant are more or less yellow.

41.text: When shown both green and yellow, the Chukchee are able to distinguish

42.text: between them; but generally they apply one term to both colors, and in

43.text: ordinary conversation always confound the two.
